 Beshear Says 80,000 Kentuckians Have Lost SNAP Benefits Following Federal Changes
 by 
 News Edge Newsroom 
 October 18, 2026 
 Governor Andy Beshear says more than 80,000 Kentuckians, including nearly 25,000 children and more than 6,500 seniors, have lost access to federal food assistance after President Donald Trump and Congress enacted changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.
 During his Thursday Team Kentucky update, Beshear called on federal officials to reverse the changes, saying they are increasing food insecurity at a time when families are already struggling with higher living expenses.
 https://dehayf5mhw1h7.cloudfront.net/wp-content/uploads/sites/2352/2026/10/19012013/Wireready_10-19-2026-01-20-12_A116_20261019011344726-1.mp3 
 click to download audio Beshear said 24,655 Kentucky children and 6,572 seniors have lost access to SNAP, commonly known as food stamps.
 The governor also said children losing SNAP eligibility could face additional consequences because the program can help establish eligibility for other nutrition assistance, including free school meals and summer electronic benefit programs.
 https://dehayf5mhw1h7.cloudfront.net/wp-content/uploads/sites/2352/2026/10/19012013/Wireready_10-19-2026-01-20-12_A116_20261019011344726-2.mp3 
 click to download audio The changes stem from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Trump signed into law last year.
 The legislation expanded work requirements for certain adults, tightened eligibility provisions, changed benefit calculations, and shifted additional administrative and benefit costs to state governments.
 Supporters argued the changes were necessary to encourage employment, strengthen program accountability, and reduce federal spending. Opponents maintain that the restrictions remove food assistance from vulnerable households and increase financial pressure on states.
 The Congressional Budget Office projected that the legislation would reduce federal SNAP spending by approximately $211 billion over 10 years.
 Kentucky began implementing expanded SNAP work requirements November 1, 2025, several months after the federal legislation became law.
 Under the revised rules, certain adults ages 18 through 64 must work, volunteer, or participate in approved employment and training activities for at least 80 hours per month to continue receiving benefits beyond three months in a 36-month period, unless they qualify for an exemption.
 The legislation expanded the age range covered by those requirements and eliminated certain previous exemptions, including those for veterans, people experiencing homelessness, and some former foster care youth.
 Other provisions, including changes to state funding responsibilities, are being phased in separately.
 According to Kentucky data, 1,702 people in Caldwell County, or 13.5% of the county’s population, participate in SNAP. In Christian County, it’s 13.3%. Todd County is 11.9%, and Trigg County is 10.8%.
